method: Complete candidate survey followed by individual editorial choices and written reasons, applied to the existing complete guide to keep it within 300 quotations. All verified authorized selections included. Priority given to foundational teachings, substantive explanations, necessary qualifications, distinctive applications, narrative examples and thematic breadth across the necessity and purpose of symbolic language, scriptural signs and stories, cosmological images, letters, numbers and colors, recurring natural figures such as light, water, fire, gardens, trees and mirrors, and the turn from interpretation to spiritual transformation. Neither citation count nor source order used as a ranking rule. The existing reading arc is retained.

selected.text: Do not worship the Lantern—worship the light
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s counsel not to worship the Lantern but the light; a concise and memorable safeguard against confusing form with reality.

selected.text: The fragrance of the rose leads man to the Garden.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s saying that the fragrance of the rose leads man to the Garden; a concise image of a sign leading to its source.

selected.text: Behold the Tree and its fruits. They are before your faces.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s call to behold the Tree and its fruits before one’s face; a concise test of recognition.

selected.text: The miracles of Christ were spiritual teachings, not literal.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s brief statement that the miracles of Christ were spiritual teachings, not literal; connects the guide to its neighboring subject of miracles.

selected.text: The story about the dove is simply a metaphor. No dove came down.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s statement that the story of the dove is simply a metaphor and no dove came down; a final plain safeguard against literal reading.

selected.text: the bird of your soul would not be contained in the cage of the body
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image of the bird of the soul not contained in the cage of the body; a brief, memorable figure for the soul.

selected.text: The wolves of the world have torn apart and beheaded the true Josephs.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s lament that the wolves of the world have beheaded the true Josephs; applies the Joseph image to persecution.

selected.text: Until the sun rises in the West, the door of repentance will remain open.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s statement that until the sun rises in the West the door of repentance remains open; preserves a traditional eschatological sign.

selected.text: as a lamp unto the darkened world and as a sun unto the realm of knowledge
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s brief image of one who is a lamp to the darkened world and a sun to the realm of knowledge; a concise light figure.

selected.text: And verily the number of "Lord" corresponds to the seven letters - ponder this
selected.reason: The Báb’s note that the number of “Lord” corresponds to seven letters; a brief instance of number and letter correspondence.

selected.text: In the Torah and Gospel, the divine Kingdom is likened to a garden and vineyard
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s note that the Torah and Gospel liken the divine Kingdom to a garden and vineyard; anchors garden imagery in scripture.

selected.text: that thou mayest drink of the Kawthar of the spirit and taste of the fruit of light
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s wish that the hearer drink of the Kawthar of the spirit and taste the fruit of light; joins river and fruit imagery.

selected.text: O God! These children are like unto pearls. Rear them in the shells of Thy Providence.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer for children likened to pearls reared in the shells of Providence; a brief devotional use of the pearl image.

selected.text: "When I ride on it, it is the Ark of Noah. This aeroplane will become the Ark of Noah."
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s remark that the aeroplane He rides becomes the Ark of Noah; a vivid instance of symbolic reading of a modern object.

selected.text: His days were but as the days of roses - thus was it ordained by the hidden Pen of might
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s line that His days were as the days of roses, ordained by the hidden Pen; a brief image of transience.

selected.text: the bird symbolizes an earthly man, who received spiritual education through the Christ
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining that the bird symbolizes an earthly man who received spiritual education through Christ; a concise key to a Gospel image.

selected.text: Lord! Make their hearts pure mirrors reflecting and displaying the lights of Your oneness
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer that hearts become pure mirrors displaying the lights of oneness; a brief devotional form of the mirror image.

selected.text: Then did the Beauty mount the saddle of light, even as the Spirit mounted the mighty throne.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Beauty mounting the saddle of light as the Spirit mounted the throne; a brief visionary image.

selected.text: This is the Lote-Tree wherein burneth the Fire of God; hasten ye unto it, O people of glory!
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Lote-Tree wherein burneth the Fire of God, with a call to hasten to it; a direct appeal through the burning-bush image.

selected.text: O Mystery of Ta-Ha and Temple of Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, and the mercy of God and His blessings
selected.reason: The Báb’s Ziyaratu’l-Hajja addressing the Mystery of Ta-Ha and Temple of Kaf-Ha-Ya-‘Ayn-Sad; shows the Qur’an’s disconnected letters used as titles of address in a visitation prayer.

selected.text: The Tree needs rain, and when the rain falls whether it is warm or cold it does not matter.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the Tree that needs rain whether it is warm or cold; a simple image of receptivity regardless of form.

selected.text: there is a Garden of God. Human beings are trees growing therein. The Gardener is Our Father.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s statement that human beings are trees in the Garden of God whose Gardener is our Father; a concise foundational image.

selected.text: You are two birds of one nest, and two fledglings of one dwelling, and two moths of one flame.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describing two souls as two birds of one nest and two moths of one flame; a concise image of unity.

selected.text: Consider man as a sword: while it remains in its sheath, its quality remains hidden and concealed.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh comparing man to a sword whose quality is hidden while it remains in its sheath; a concise image of latent capacity.

selected.text: The spider busies itself catching flies, while the divine Phoenix of Qaf hunts for inner meanings.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh contrasting the spider catching flies with the divine Phoenix of Qaf hunting for inner meanings; a memorable image of the seeker after meaning.

selected.text: The hand is veiled, yet the pen writes as bidden; … The horse leaps forward, yet the rider's hidden
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Bride means Christ; Bridegroom, the cause of God. … The first is faith; the second, action and deeds
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining bride and bridegroom as Christ and the Cause of God, and faith and deeds; a compact interpretive key.

selected.text: I liken you to the pupil of the eye. You are black and it is black, yet it becomes the focus of light.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá to Louis Gregory likening him to the pupil of the eye, black yet the focus of light; a memorable personal application of symbolic speech.

selected.text: When one enters a rose garden, one inhales sweet fragrances, but in a dunghill one encounters foul smells.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s contrast of sweet fragrances in a rose garden with foul smells in a dunghill; a brief image of environment and influence.

selected.text: This seed may be likened to the perfect soul; the souls of men in general are as the leaves and the flowers.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening the seed to the perfect soul and the leaves and flowers to souls in general; a concise image of relationship.

selected.text: the occurrence is correctly stated and really happened. In the spiritual significance, we find that Abel represents the Divine Law or Religion, and Cain the human nature
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá teaching that Cain and Abel’s story really happened while Abel represents the Divine Law and Cain human nature; shows historical and spiritual meanings coexisting.

selected.text: The dawn hath broken and the moon hath appeared, and the Sun crieth out: "To Me, to Me, O peoples of the earth!"
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s dawn breaking and the Sun crying “To Me, to Me, O peoples of the earth!”; a vivid personified image of the call.

selected.text: In short, one finds on this divine table all kinds of spiritual food which constitutes the real Supper of the Lord
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the divine table bearing all spiritual food as the real Supper of the Lord; returns the image to transformation and helps close the guide.

selected.text: These are symbols. Always, hair is the symbol of the Glory of GOD, and the Face is the symbol of the Beauty
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s answer that hair is always the symbol of the Glory of God and the Face of the Beauty; closes the opening arc with a direct key to a recurring image.

selected.text: Through one blessed word He caused the new creation to blaze like a sphere of fire and sent it forth with a mission.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh describing how one blessed word caused the new creation to blaze like a sphere of fire; links Word and fire.

selected.text: when that drop passed beyond the realm of contingent being it hastened to the infinite expanse and became a boundless sea
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s drop that passed beyond contingent being and became a boundless sea; a concise figure of the soul’s transformation.

selected.text: The name is like a chalice and the attribute like the wine. I hope that these two cups may overflow with that divine wine.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening the name to a chalice and the attribute to the wine; a concise image of form and content.

selected.text: You are on the seashore and on the shore of a tumultuous sea. When you gaze upon that sea, remember the Sea of the Covenant.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s counsel that one gazing on a tumultuous sea should remember the Sea of the Covenant; a practical habit of reading nature as sign.

selected.text: and cast away thy robe, tear asunder the veils, and raise the banner of the righteous. Be a light that shineth forth in the darkness of the night, and set the world aflame
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s call to tear the veils and be a light that shines in the darkness and sets the world aflame; applies light and veil imagery to action.

selected.text: The Tree of Anisa is the blessed tree which hath flourished in the Most Great Paradise and casteth its shadow upon all regions
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: Hearken thou unto the call of thy Lord from the right side of the Throne, from behind a thousand veils of luminous silk damask.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s call from the Throne behind a thousand veils of luminous silk damask; a concise image of veiled revelation.

selected.text: Thus hath crowed the Cock of the Divine Throne, and sung the Dove, and warbled the Nightingale of Paradise, did ye but hear it.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Cock of the Divine Throne, Dove and Nightingale of Paradise, did ye but hear it; a brief chorus of bird symbols with a call to hear.

selected.text: If a tree was fruit-bearing in the past but is now dead, then it is no longer a tree. Today, it must manifest harvests and fruits.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on a once fruitful tree that is now dead and no longer a tree, since today it must bear fruit; a pointed test of living meaning.

selected.text: This goodly Tree, though hidden at first, will erelong envelop the whole world, and its leaves and branches will reach the heavens.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s goodly Tree, hidden at first, that will envelop the world; an image of hidden growth and disclosure.

selected.text: We have ordained for each one a haykal from Our presence, the like of which all the worlds cannot equal even a single letter thereof
selected.reason: The Báb ordaining a haykal for each one, not equalled by the worlds in a single letter; shows the talisman form as symbol.

selected.text: Serpent is the symbol of religion, because a serpent swallows everything; so the religion of God swallows up, or removes every doubt
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the serpent as symbol of religion swallowing every doubt; shows a symbol with multiple valences.

selected.text: and the Bird of Light warbles upon the branches of the Tree of Sinai, and the Cock of Glorification sings in the gardens of Divine Unity
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Bird of Light on the Tree of Sinai and Cock of Glorification in the gardens of Unity; extends bird and tree imagery.

selected.text: and guide these two longing hearts to the rose-garden of inner meanings and realities. Lead these two fish to the sweet waters of guidance, and bring these two gazelles of the desert of unity to the meadow of Thy bounty
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer leading two hearts to the rose garden of inner meanings, two fish to sweet waters and two gazelles to the meadow of bounty; a gentle devotional use of nature symbols.

selected.text: The intent of "heaven" is not this boundless space, but rather the intent of heaven is the world of reality which is higher than all worlds
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá stating that heaven means not boundless space but the world of reality higher than all worlds; a direct correction of a literal reading.

selected.text: He leads forth the army of love in the field of endeavor and eliminates the forces of enmity, hostility and rancor from the face of the earth.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on One who leads the army of love and removes enmity from the earth; closes with symbolism turned to transformation of hearts.

selected.text: I beseech Thee by Thy Fig which was raised up in the Most Exalted Paradise, and by the Olive Tree which stood tall before the crimson chambers
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh beseeching God by the Fig raised in Paradise and the Olive before the crimson chambers; complements the Fig and Olive commentary.

selected.text: I praise Thee for having ordained the Fountain of Life in the Garden of Good-Pleasure, wherein Thou didst join together fire and water and unite them through Thy power, such that they shall never be parted throughout the eternity of Thy might and the perpetuity of Thy sovereignty. Thou didst appoint as keeper of this Fountain the serpent of Thy power and the snake of Thy protection, and didst breathe into this keeper from the essence of Thy spirit, such that all things die save it, and all things sleep save it, as if it were made a sign of movement, for within it is passion and rapture and agitation.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Tablet of the Hair on the Fountain of Life uniting fire and water, kept by the serpent of His power; a striking union of opposed elements.

selected.text: "Once again the dove of eternity hath descended from the rizwan of nearness to sing the long-forgotten melody in this gloomy and disastrous age.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quoting the dove of eternity descending from the rizwan of nearness to sing a forgotten melody; brings the dove image into a later age.

selected.text: My hair is My Phoenix. Therefore hath it set itself upon the blazing fire of My Face and receiveth sustenance from the garden of My Countenance.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s hair as His Phoenix sustained by the blazing fire of His Face; extends the hair and phoenix figures.

selected.text: The Tongue of Grandeur has in all times summoned the servants to the living waters … summoning them to the Hidden Name and the Treasured Secret
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Tongue of Grandeur summoning the servants to the living waters and the Hidden Name; brings water imagery into the call to recognition.

selected.text: the belly of the whale represents the darkness of the world of nature, and deliverance and salvation from this darkness is a boundless wilderness
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá interpreting the belly of the whale as the darkness of the world of nature; a concise key to the Jonah story.

selected.text: The mountains being shaken before the coming of the messenger means that great peoples -- great as mountains -- are shaken and become transplanted.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá interpreting the shaking of mountains as great peoples shaken and transplanted; a concise key to prophetic imagery.

selected.text: Him Who was named the Quarter of Eternity, then the Sinai of the Cloud, then the Horeb of Origination, then the Crimson Paran, then the Sacred Precinct
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh naming the One called Quarter of Eternity, Sinai of the Cloud, Horeb of Origination and Crimson Paran; shows sacred places used as titles of spiritual station.

selected.text: which is like the blessed Tree whose "root is firmly fixed in the earth and whose branch reacheth unto heaven" and "yielding its fruit in all seasons."
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá citing the blessed Tree whose root is firm and branch reaches heaven, yielding fruit in all seasons; links the guide’s tree to Qur’anic wording.

selected.text: to that which I have witnessed, and sufficient art Thou as a witness unto me. Know thou that God hath said: "We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves until it becomes clear to them that this is the Truth
selected.reason: The Báb citing the verse “We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in themselves”; grounds the reading of signs in outward and inward worlds.

selected.text: The cause of God is like unto a house. As long as man has not entered therein he does not know what it contains. In the house there are many precious jewels, many rare objects the like of which can be found nowhere in the world
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening the Cause of God to a house whose jewels are unknown until one enters; an image of knowledge by entering.

selected.text: The Kingdom of God is like unto this garden. It contains many kind of trees. In due season the trees must not only produce leaves and blossoms, but fruits.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening the Kingdom of God to a garden whose trees must produce fruits, not only leaves and blossoms; supports the garden theme with a practical demand.

selected.text: Then, further, there are certain signs and allegories recorded in the Scriptures relative to the coming of the Messiah. These signs are written in symbols
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá stating that the signs and allegories concerning the Messiah’s coming are written in symbols; links symbolism to prophecy.

selected.text: Do you not see the bird soaring in the atmosphere of heaven, how We grasp it at the Gate to teach you the stages of the leaves from the Camphor Tree in truth?
selected.reason: The Báb pointing to a bird soaring in heaven and grasped at the Gate to teach the stages of the leaves of the Camphor Tree; shows a natural image turned into a lesson in spiritual stages.

selected.text: The nightingales sang the melody of unity and expressed mysteries and meanings. … It became a garden of supreme paradise, and the rose garden sought adornment
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s nightingales singing the melody of unity and mysteries, the garden becoming a supreme paradise; extends the guide’s garden imagery.

selected.text: The Dove of Holiness has warbled in these gardens, and the Lions of Truth have roared in these thickets, and the Whales of Knowledge have swum in these pools.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s Dove of Holiness, Lions of Truth and Whales of Knowledge in gardens, thickets and pools; the fuller of two similar animal triads.

selected.text: As long as you are on the shore - or as long as the sands of your sins are on the shore - the waves of the sea will wash them for the sea will wash everything.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the waves of the sea washing away the sands of sins while one is on the shore; a gentle image of forgiveness.

selected.text: The sun gives light to the entire world, but its penetrating power is strongest at the equator. The divine teachings should have their strongest effect in Iran.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the sun’s strongest power at the equator applied to the divine teachings in Iran; a distinctive application of the sun image.

selected.text: Look at these white lilies---How fragrant and pure they are! an emblem of the spotless heart, a token of graceful life, typifying virginity and harmonious existence
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on white lilies as an emblem of the spotless heart and harmonious life; a direct floral emblem.

selected.text: Hell designated the heedlessness of people from God. The meaning of skin is doubts, and whenever one doubt of their doubts is taken away, a new doubt will take place.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá interpreting hell as heedlessness of God and skin as doubts that are renewed; a brief key to eschatological imagery.

selected.text: of insight, that true spirituality is like unto a lake of clear water which reflects the divine. Of such was the spirituality of Jesus Christ. There is another kind which is like a mirage, seeming to be spiritual when it is not
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá contrasting true spirituality as a clear lake reflecting the divine with false spirituality as a mirage; a necessary qualification against counterfeit meaning.

selected.text: The banquet of divine bounty is spread to overflowing and festive celebrations are in full splendour in the meadow for the chalice of Jamshid is being carried round!
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s banquet of divine bounty with the chalice of Jamshid carried round; links the Jamshid cup to celebration.

selected.text: Verily the ocean surgeth, the ark is the way and entering it is to be lifted up towards Him. The clouds raineth, the meadows rejoiceth, and the sweet savours wafteth.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s surging ocean whose ark is the way and whose entry is to be lifted toward God; reads Noah’s ark as a path.

selected.text: God beareth witness that the ocean surgeth, and the breeze bloweth, and the Light shineth forth, and the Fire calleth aloud, and the Sun speaketh, and the Moon uttereth.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s witness that the ocean surges, the Fire calls and the Sun and Moon speak; a chorus of elements as voices.

selected.text: thy lamentation, and at dawn thy moaning." Whereupon it cried out saying: "O Lord of the worlds! the ungodly have sunk Thy crimson Ark and slaughtered Thy white She-Camel, and desired to extinguish Thy light through the fire of hatred that blazed in their hearts
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s lament that the ungodly sank the crimson Ark and slaughtered the white She-Camel; shows Qur’anic signs applied to persecution.

selected.text: Some individuals are like rootless plants, they are pulled out by the slightest breeze. But those who are steadfast are like trees that have strong roots and foundations.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá contrasting rootless plants pulled up by a breeze with steadfast souls like deeply rooted trees; complements the tree images with a practical application.

selected.text: A lock of My hair is My Cord. He who layeth fast hold on it shall never to all eternity go astray, for therein is his guidance to the splendours of the Light of His Beauty.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s lock of hair as His Cord, holding fast to which guides to the Light of His Beauty; complements the hair symbolism of the opening.

selected.text: there is a saying in the East by which the color white symbolizes divine will; red, divine decree and martyrdom; green, predestination; and yellow, execution of the decree
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá citing the Eastern saying that white symbolizes divine will, red decree and martyrdom, green predestination and yellow execution; the guide’s clearest key to color symbolism.

selected.text: O Lord! Make him a nightingale whose song rises in this sublime garden, a lofty tree with low-hanging fruits in this exalted paradise, and a warbling bird in these thickets
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayer that a soul become a nightingale, a fruitful tree and a warbling bird in the garden; a devotional application of garden symbols.

selected.text: Though musk and ambergris are sweet-scented and fragrant, their diffusion is confined to a limited distance. But the musk-pods of divine mysteries perfume both East and West
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá contrasting musk’s limited fragrance with the musk-pods of divine mysteries that perfume East and West; uses scent to distinguish outward and inward.

selected.text: By the locks of Thy musk-scented hair, which hath cut off the destitute dwellers of the valley of search from all hope and expectation through the majesty of a new affliction
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh swearing by the musk-scented locks that cut off the seekers in the valley of search from hope; extends the hair imagery to affliction.

selected.text: Christ is a king. His shepherd's staff, that is, his tongue, was a sword dividing the true from the false. The throne of David is not a material throne but an eternal kingdom.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá interpreting Christ’s shepherd’s staff as His tongue, a sword dividing true from false, and David’s throne as an eternal kingdom; a concise reading of messianic images.

selected.text: So in order to give any shadow of meaning to us of this Infinite, everlasting Kingdom, He compared it to this world as it would seem to a baby still in its mother's womb, etc.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the Kingdom being compared to this world as it would seem to a baby in the womb; shows comparison as the only shadow of meaning for the infinite.

selected.text: This is a remembrance from the Tree of Love which has descended upon the shore of the heart, and a fire from the treasury of nearness which is ignited in the Mount of the Tablet
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s remembrance from the Tree of Love on the shore of the heart and a fire kindled on the Mount of the Tablet; joins tree, fire and heart.

selected.text: The candle of the gathering of light was extinguished, and the bat of blindness became the wanton plaything of the arena; the sovereign of the sanctuary of honour sat upon the point
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s extinguished candle of light and the bat of blindness playing in the arena; an image of darkness when light is withdrawn.

selected.text: This meeting is like the meeting of magnet and iron, like the spring rain and pure, pristine soil, like the meeting of light and mirror, like the meeting of the breeze and trees.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening a meeting to magnet and iron, spring rain and soil, light and mirror, breeze and trees; a chain of natural similes for spiritual encounter.

selected.text: when they weep like winter clouds and laugh like spring lightning, when like trees they don the robe of the greatest gift and like flower gardens burst forth with blossoms and roses
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image of souls who weep like winter clouds, laugh like spring lightning and bloom like flower gardens; vivid seasonal similes.

selected.text: Paris is like unto a green meadow, the people are like unto the sheep, they graze in this meadow, they drink of the flowing streams. The philosophers cow-like, graze with the rest
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likening Paris to a green meadow where people and philosophers graze like sheep and cows; the guide’s closing example of symbolic perception of everyday life.

selected.text: And from this verse that says in the Torah that the Spirit of God was like a bird above the water - what is meant is the water of divine knowledge which is the cause of heavenly life.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá to a rabbi interpreting the Spirit of God like a bird above the water as the water of divine knowledge; a Torah image read through the guide’s water symbolism.

selected.text: The form of the cross is made by two lines crossing each other at right angles. It is to be found in everything--even in this piece of cloth. It is the symbol of spiritual sacrifice.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on the form of the cross found in everything as a symbol of spiritual sacrifice; complements the cross interpretation with its meaning.

selected.text: This water hath been called by all names - at times thou seest it as fire, in such wise that its roaring flame is heard; at other times thou beholdest it as light, kindled and shining.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh on a water called by all names, seen now as roaring fire and now as shining light; shows one reality taking several symbolic forms.

selected.text: Praise be to Him Who made darkness the ornament of light and thereby adorned the beauty of manifestation … as though it were the Pen of Creation moving upon the Holy Tablet in Paradise
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s Tablet of the Hair praising Him Who made darkness the ornament of light; adds a paradox to the guide’s light imagery.

selected.text: just as God says "the Kaaba is the House of God," and there is no doubt that God is none other than His creation which He has related to Himself so that all His servants might honor it
selected.reason: The Báb on the Ka‘bah called the House of God because God related it to Himself; shows how a place becomes a sign by attribution.

selected.text: of the two luminous ones, the radiant one at the dayspring of the two easts and the two wests. selected.reason: The Báb’s chain of paired images, pure water in two gulfs and fire in two trees, for the radiant one at the dayspring; shows dense symbolic pairing.

selected.text: In another sense, by the terms "sun," "moon," and "stars" are meant such laws and teachings as have been established and proclaimed in every Dispensation, such as the laws of prayer and fasting
selected.reason: Mandatory inclusion: exact selected wording lies in a catalogue-authorized paragraph of this translation version.

selected.text: This is the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and the Farthest Mosque, and "two bow-lengths or even closer" in relation to those souls who dwell in the realm of creation
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá identifying the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary, the Farthest Mosque and “two bow-lengths” in relation to souls; shows Qur’anic images applied to station.

selected.text: Reflect upon the books of old and what was revealed therein concerning the signs of the Manifestation. By God! Thou shalt find naught save symbols and allusions, if ye would but understand.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh’s counsel to reflect on the books of old, where the signs of the Manifestation prove to be symbols and allusions; frames the older scriptures as calls to understanding rather than literalism.

selected.text: Hearken ye to the rapturous melody from the Countenance of Him Who sitteth upon the Throne of Nearness, the Point of Manifestation, the Mystery of Concealment, the Hidden Secret of the Book

The truth of this saying might be that the Simurgh was an illustrious personage whose nest and dwelling place was the Caucasian clime, and through divine favors was most dignified and steadfast--that is to say, was a mighty fortress preserved and protected from the deficiencies and base qualities of human souls.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá on Mount Qaf and the Simurgh, suggesting the bird may signify an illustrious personage protected from base qualities; a cautious alternative reading of a legend.

selected.text: In reality all of these prophetic signs did come to pass, that is to say, the inner significances appeared, but not in an outward and literal sense. For instance, it was prophesied that the promised one should come from a place unknown. So the Jews said of Christ: "We know this person. He is from Nazareth. We know his house; whereas the promised one is to come from a place unknown." In truth Christ did come from a place unknown -- for his reality -- the Christ reality -- came in the body of Jesus. Though the body of Jesus came from Nazareth, yet the Christianity -- the spirit of Christ, -- being divine, was placeless.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining that prophecies came to pass in inner significance, as Christ came from a place unknown though Jesus came from Nazareth; a substantive example of spiritual fulfilment.

selected.text: Thus was the Most Great Book completed, and by it were adorned all who are in earth and heaven, that the Daysprings of negation might witness at the station of annihilation what the Tree of Divine decree hath witnessed in the luminous spot, and might turn towards the Dawning-Place of the Call at the station of evanescence - that place wherein the Most Exalted Word donned the crimson robe in the kingdom of creation, and that the people of the Kingdom might hear the melodies of the leaves suspended upon the Tree beyond which there is no passing, in remembrance of this Remembrance Who hath appeared with the standards of verses to all who are in the heavens and the earth.
selected.reason: Bahá’u’lláh on the Most Great Book completed, the Most Exalted Word donning the crimson robe and melodies of leaves on the Tree beyond which there is no passing; a sustained cluster of the guide’s symbols.

selected.text: Say: They who hold in their hands white diamonds and engrave upon them "God is Most Glorious" are like unto those who glorify God, their Lord, the All-Merciful, and who never cease. Say: They who hold in their hands yellow topaz and engrave upon them "God is Most Exalted" are like unto those who thank God, their Lord, the All-Merciful, at all times, and who glorify Him with His praise. And they who possess a green emerald and engrave thereon "God is Most Powerful" shall be rewarded on the Day of Resurrection like unto those who proclaim the unity of God at all times and never grow weary. Say: They who possess a red ruby and engrave thereon "God is Most Enduring" shall be rewarded on the Day of Resurrection like unto those who magnify God at all times and never tire
selected.reason: The Báb linking white diamond, yellow topaz, green emerald and red ruby, each engraved with a divine phrase, to forms of glorification; distinctive application of gems and colors as devotional symbols.

selected.text: Say: The first pillar remembereth its Lord and saith: "God beareth witness that there is no God but Him, the Lord of all worlds." selected.text: And as for the woman who will flee into the wilderness, mentioned in the twelfth chapter of the Book of Revelation - "And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet" - this woman signifieth the Law of God, for in the terminology of the Holy Books, it is a metaphor for the Law of God, which is here expressed as a woman. And the two luminaries, the sun and the moon - that is, the Turkish and Persian kingdoms - are under the shadow of the Law of God. The sun is the emblem of the Persian state, and the moon, being a crescent, is the emblem of the Turkish state. And the twelve crowns are the twelve Imams who, like the apostles, supported the Religion
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reading the woman clothed with the sun in Revelation as the Law of God, with the sun, moon and twelve crowns given specific meanings; a detailed worked example of scriptural symbolism.

selected.text: Accordingly, when God, glorified and exalted be He, desired to explain the magnificent bounties and abundant favors ordained in His wondrous paradise and beauteous gardens in the kingdom of His holiness and the seat of His intimate companionship, He cast those spiritual realities and divine intellectual essences into molds of forms such as houris, palaces, flowers, rivers, pools, gardens, and groves, that listeners might become aware of those abundant bounties and multiplying favors, of eternal happiness and holy blessed life in the next world, and of divine knowledge and spiritual delights in this first life. This is the wisdom of what God hath sent down in the Qur'an through the breath of the All-Merciful.
selected.reason: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining that God cast spiritual realities into forms such as houris, palaces, rivers and gardens so listeners might grasp them; a foundational statement of why paradise is pictured.

selected.text: That which was revealed in the first year is the fruits of the Paradise of the Divine Identity, pertaining to Muhammad (peace be upon Him), and His star pertaineth to the land of Persia, wherein it must be recorded in a book containing the four rivers of divine manifestation. … That which was revealed in the second year is the fruits of the Tree of Divinity, pertaining to Ali (peace be upon Him), and His star pertaineth to the land of Iraq, to be written in a book containing the four stations of creation, sustenance, death and life. … That which was revealed in the third year is the fruits of the Paradise of Oneness, pertaining to Fatima (peace be upon Her), and Her star pertaineth to the land of Azerbaijan, wherein it must be recorded in a book containing the four stations
selected.reason: The Báb’s Letter to Quddus assigning the revelations of successive years to fruits, stars and lands; shows symbolic correspondences across time and place.

selected.text: But when you undertake to express these intelligible realities, you have no recourse but to cast them in the mould of the sensible, for outwardly there is nothing beyond the sensible. Thus, when you wish to express the reality of the spirit and its conditions and degrees, you are obliged to describe them in terms of sensible things, since outwardly there exists nothing but the sensible. For example, grief and happiness are intelligible things, but when you wish to express these spiritual conditions you say, "My heart became heavy", or "My heart was uplifted", although one's heart is not literally made heavy or lifted up. Rather, it is a spiritual or intelligible condition, the expression of which requires the use of sensible terms. Another example is when you say, "So-and-so has greatly advanced", although he has remained in the same place, or "So-and-so has a high position", whereas, like everyone else, he continues to walk upon the earth. selected.text: Whatever there is in the world of contingency is a symbol of the spiritual world; whatever there is on the earth is a symbol of heavenly things. For example: In the spiritual world there is the light of guidance, in the outer world there is the lamp, its symbol. In the divine world there is love, symbolized in the material world by magnetism. So there are four seasons in the perishable, outer world-spring, which brings the vegetables, refreshes the animals, and promises fruits; summer, which charges the trees with fruits; then follows, the autumn, after which comes the winter, when the trees are bare and empty. Such is the condition of the spiritual world, which has its four seasons-spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
selected.reason: Explains correspondence between earthly symbols and spiritual realities.
